card.p: Kestrel Systems · Leadership team · Illustrative worked example

card.h1: A worked example, not real company data

ul.li: Kestrel Systems is fictional. Every figure, customer, and quote was invented to demonstrate the structure of a leadership QBR.

One dataset runs the whole deck. The ARR bridge, the segment ledger, the account counts, and the retention rates are all derived from the same beginning-of-quarter book, so every slide reconciles to every other.
Three kinds of statement are labeled: figures from the fictional dataset, assumptions used to project (marked as such), and the industry benchmarks on slide 5, which are real and cited.
Profile used throughout: vertical SaaS for mid-market food and beverage manufacturers. $48.2M ARR, 212 employees, Series C.

card.h1: We missed by $0.7M, and expansion covered most of a $0.9M new-logo hole

ul.li: Closed Q3 at $48.2M ARR against a $48.9M plan. A $0.7M miss, 1.4%.
New logo is the whole problem: $2.1M against a $3.0M plan. Nothing else missed by more than $0.3M.
Expansion beat plan by $0.6M, its third straight quarter of doing so, and absorbed two thirds of the new-logo shortfall.
Gross churn and contraction together ran $1.4M against a $1.0M plan. Half of that $1.4M came from SMB, which is only 14% of the book.
The decision this quarter is whether we keep selling to a segment we cannot keep.

ul.li: $48.2M ARR — up 7.3% on Q2's $44.9M, up 29% year over year
96.9% quarterly gross revenue retention — 88% annualized, down from 91% a year ago
102.7% quarterly net revenue retention — 111% annualized, down from 114%
$2.40 of sales and marketing per $1 of new-customer ARR — up from $1.95 last year
19 months of runway on $31M cash, at a 1.5x burn multiple

card.h1: Growth is ahead of the market; retention is behind it
card.p: Kestrel's invented annualized figures against published 2025 private B2B SaaS medians.

ul.li: Growth: 29% against a 26% median
Net revenue retention: 111% against a 101% median. This is the metric leadership tends to quote
Gross revenue retention: 88% against a 91% median, and 90–91% at every contract size below $250k. We are below market on the metric that measures whether customers stay
New-customer CAC ratio: $2.40 against a $2.00 median. A fifth less efficient than the market
Expansion share of new ARR: ours is 55% ($2.6M of $4.7M), against 40% industry-wide and above 50% for companies over $50M ARR. We are already living off the installed base

card.h1: NRR is a blended number, and blending is hiding the problem
card.p: All rates below are for the quarter, measured on the $44.9M of ARR on the books at July 1. Gross retention is beginning ARR less churn and contraction, over beginning ARR. Net adds expansion back. Annualized figures elsewhere in the deck are the quarterly rate compounded four times, which assumes the rate holds.

ul.li: Enterprise (over $100k ACV): 98.9% gross, 106.2% net. 137 customers, $27.4M, 61% of ARR.
Mid-market ($25k–$100k): 96.4% gross, 100.9% net. 224 customers, $11.2M, 25% of ARR.
SMB (under $25k): 88.9% gross, 90.5% net. 420 customers, $6.3M, 14% of ARR.
Weighted by beginning ARR these give the blended 96.9% gross and 102.7% net exactly. SMB net retention is below 100%, so that book shrinks every quarter with no one doing anything wrong.

card.h1: SMB is 14% of revenue and 54% of the logos

ul.li: 420 SMB customers at an average $15k contract. 54% of our 781 logos, 14% of ARR.
They filed 46% of support tickets last quarter and consumed 38% of CSM hours.
Fully loaded cost to serve is roughly $5.1k per account per year against a $15k contract, leaving about $9.9k of annual contribution.

Assumption, not a measurement: 31 of the 420 SMB accounts churned this quarter, 7.4%. Held constant that is 26% a year and an average life of 3.8 years, which values a new SMB account at about $37k of lifetime contribution against $18k of blended acquisition cost. That is 2.1x, and the 2024 cohort came in under 1.0x.
The six largest enterprise expansions this quarter totaled $1.2M, about $200k each. Each one was worth more than a dozen new SMB logos.

card.h1: Why SMB customers leave: we asked the last 40

ul.li: 17 of 40 — never got live. Churned with under 20% of licensed seats ever activated. Median time from signature to first production work order: 51 days.
11 of 40 — lost their champion. One plant manager bought it, they left, nobody inherited it.
7 of 40 — price at renewal, almost all after a seat-count true-up they had not anticipated.
5 of 40 — genuine product gaps, four of them multi-site reporting.
These are the last 40 SMB accounts to churn, spanning two quarters. The top two causes are 70% of them, and neither is about the product. They are both about the first sixty days.

card.h1: Onboarding is the single highest-leverage thing we are bad at

ul.li: Median time to first production use: 51 days enterprise, 44 days SMB. Target is 30.
Customers live inside 30 days renew at 94%. Customers who take more than 60 renew at 67%.
We have 3 implementation engineers for 781 customers. Every deal over $60k queues behind another deal.
The queue is why SMB onboarding defaulted to self-service, which is exactly the cohort that cannot self-serve.
This is a staffing decision we have deferred for four quarters, not a discovery.

card.h1: What went right, and it was not small

ul.li: Downtime Analytics reached $4.1M ARR in its fourth quarter, attached to 34% of enterprise accounts. Fastest module ramp in company history.
Two expansions over $400k: a regional dairy group went from 3 to 11 plants, and a bakery co-op added compliance reporting across its footprint. Both sit inside the $2.0M of enterprise expansion.
Enterprise sales cycle fell from 141 to 118 days after we moved security review to the front of the process.
ARR per employee rose to $227k from $198k, on flat headcount since March.

card.h1: The Q4 pipeline does not currently support the plan

ul.li: Q4 new-logo plan is $3.4M. Qualified pipeline is $9.2M, or 2.7x coverage, against the 3.5x our 29% win rate requires.
The gap is $2.7M of pipeline, which at current create rates is about five weeks of top-of-funnel.
Three renewals over $500k land in Q4, totaling $2.8M. One, a 14-plant protein processor, is amber on the multi-site reporting gap.
Committed EU data residency ships in the December release. Slipping it costs a $740k deal and credibility with two others.

card.h1: Three decisions we need from this room
card.p: Each has an owner, a cost, and a number it is accountable for.

ol.li: Move six CSMs from pooled SMB coverage to named enterprise accounts. Net headcount change: zero. SMB moves to in-app onboarding and a tech-touch motion. Target: enterprise gross retention from 98.9% to 99.4% a quarter, 96% to 98% annualized.

Raise the SMB price floor from $9k to $14k and launch a $3,600 self-serve tier. About 40 accounts sit below the new floor, averaging $10k. We lose $400k of ARR a year and save $204k of cost to serve, so this costs us roughly $196k of contribution every year it holds. It does not pay for itself. What it buys is capacity: 40 accounts, a tenth of the SMB book, come off human coverage and move to the self-serve tier, where anyone who converts returns revenue at close to zero service cost. Accountable number: the 90-day conversion mix, not a payback date.
Fund four implementation engineers, $620k annualized. Target: median time to first use from 51 days to 30 by the end of Q1.

card.h1: What changes if we do all three

ul.li: Gross retention from 88% to 92% annualized by Q2 FY27, driven by enterprise coverage and faster onboarding.
New-customer CAC ratio from $2.40 to $2.05 as we stop paying full sales cost to win $15k contracts.
Logo count falls about 5%, from 781 to roughly 740, and ARR growth dips to about 24% for two quarters before reaccelerating. We should decide today that we are willing to say that to the board.

Net new cost: $620k of payroll plus about $196k a year of contribution we give up at the price floor. Against that, four points of gross retention on a $50M base is worth about $2.0M a year. That is a modeled outcome, not a commitment, and it assumes the retention curve behaves as it has.

card.h1: What we are accepting if we are wrong

ul.li: The self-serve tier cannibalizes mid-market. Mitigation: feature gate at three sites, and review the conversion mix in 90 days. If conversion is weak, the price floor is a straight $196k-a-year revenue decision with only capacity to show for it.
Implementation hires take a quarter to become productive. True. The retention benefit lands in Q2 FY27, not Q4.
SMB is a farm system for future mid-market accounts. Partly true: 9 of our 224 mid-market customers started in SMB. The self-serve tier keeps that path open at a tenth of the cost.

The lifetime math rests on a constant churn rate. If SMB churn is accelerating rather than steady, every payback number on slide 7 is optimistic and the case for the price floor gets stronger, not weaker.

card.h1: Decisions, owners, and the next checkpoint

ul.li: CSM reallocation — VP Customer Success — decision today, effective November 1
SMB pricing floor and self-serve tier — CRO with Finance — decision today, in market January 15
Implementation hiring — VP Services — approve budget today, all four seated by December 31
Q4 pipeline gap — CRO — $2.7M plan back to this group in two weeks
Next checkpoint: monthly retention review starting November 15, with time to first use reported as a headline metric alongside ARR

brief.instruction: Write like a sharp operator briefing peers who already know the business — direct, numerate, no throat-clearing. About 65 words per slide; the template holds median 58, p90 99, so budget 58 and go to 99 only on a deliberately text-only slide. Every bullet must carry a fact, a number, or a judgment. If a line could appear in any company's QBR, cut it. Numbers are load-bearing: state them with their comparison (against plan, against last quarter, against benchmark) rather than alone. Titles state the finding, not the topic — "SMB is 14% of revenue and 54% of the logos", never "SMB Analysis". Keep the outline's titles; they are the argument. Vary sentence and paragraph length. Never the "Bold term: explanation" pattern as a whole-slide format, though a bold lead-in label inside a list item is fine and used deliberately here. No signposting ("Let's explore", "In this section"). No sweeping openers or inspirational closers — start and end on substance. None of the "not just X — it's Y" contrast family. No em dashes in body copy. Do not soften the bad news. Leadership audiences trust a deck that names a miss in the first sentence.

Restrained consulting grammar: hairline-ruled ledgers, KPI plates, unframed native charts each with a caption stating what it means. One accent color marks the single thing the audience should notice per slide; status chips carry the only other color. Data is the argument on slides 3, 4 and 6. Slide 3's plan-versus-actual table and slide 6's segment ledger are the deck's reconciliation artifacts: render them as precise ruled tables with numeric columns right-aligned on their digits, never as decoration, and never abbreviate a figure in a way that breaks the arithmetic. Slide 4's ARR bridge and slide 6's retention comparison get full weight as native charts. Slide 8 (churn reasons) wants a simple ranked bar or ruled ledger, not a pie. Slide 11 (the three decisions) is the deck's climax: numbered, scannable, each decision visually equal. Slide 2 is the example disclaimer — plain, quiet, unmissable. No imagery that dresses it up. Imagery is contextual scene-setting only, in the template's documentary and flat-illustration registers: food and beverage manufacturing floors, production lines, maintenance work, logistics. Never present a generated image as evidence of a customer, a person, an event, or a result, and never attach a fictional company's name or logo to a photograph. Most data slides need no image at all; let paper and rules carry them. Use the dark wave field for the cover and at most two act breaks so the deck has pauses.

Kestrel Systems and every customer, figure, quote, and outcome attributed to it are invented for this prototype. The disclaimer on slide 2 is the single clear label; do not repeat it on later slides and do not add hedging language that undercuts the worked example. The dataset is closed and internally consistent. Do not add, round, or reinterpret any figure that is not in the outline, because every number depends on the others. The canonical basis, for reference while writing: beginning ARR $44.9M (enterprise $27.4M / mid-market $11.2M / SMB $6.3M); churn plus contraction $1.4M ($0.30M / $0.40M / $0.70M); expansion $2.6M ($2.00M / $0.50M / $0.10M); new logo $2.1M; closing ARR $48.2M against a $48.9M plan. Quarterly gross retention is beginning ARR less churn and contraction over beginning ARR; net adds expansion. Weighted by beginning ARR the segments give exactly 96.9% gross and 102.7% net. Annualized figures are the quarterly rate raised to the fourth power: 88% gross, 111% net. Account counts are 137 / 224 / 420 at $200k / $50k / $15k average ACV, which multiply back to the segment ARR and sum to 781 logos and $44.9M. The SMB price floor does not pay for itself, and no slide may imply otherwise. Forty accounts at $10k is $400k of recurring ARR given up against $204k of recurring cost to serve saved (40 x $5.1k), a standing cost of about $196k a year. Lost ARR recurs, so it can never be recovered by a one-time or multi-quarter cost saving; do not write a payback period, a break-even, or a recovery date for it anywhere in the deck. Keep the three kinds of statement distinct. Dataset figures are stated flat. Projections that rest on an assumption — the annualized rates, the 3.8-year SMB life, the $2.0M of protected ARR — must keep the outline's assumption language; never promote one to a measured result. Interpretation is written as judgment, not as arithmetic. The only real, citable facts are the industry benchmarks on slide 5, from published 2025 B2B SaaS surveys. Keep those exact, keep them clearly distinct from Kestrel's invented figures, and do not add any benchmark, market statistic, or third-party comparison that is not already in the outline. Never imply the deck was built from a supplied document, dataset, or client asset. None was provided.
